solution.concept_anchor: Select Committee vs Standing Committee classification
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because Select Committees deal with Bills, which are a continuous parliamentary function, making students assume they are standing bodies.
elimination_logic: Eliminate any option classifying Select Committees as Standing Committees — they dissolve after submitting their report on the specific Bill.
Eliminate options that conflate Financial Committees with Ad Hoc bodies — PAC, Estimates Committee, and CPU are Standing Committees.
Identify that the defining feature of Ad Hoc committees is their temporary, purpose-specific constitution — Select and Joint Committees fit this perfectly.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently classify Select Committees as Standing Committees because they handle the important legislative function of Bill scrutiny and appear 'permanent' in name. The trap exploits the misconception that committees with formal powers (summoning witnesses, clause-by-clause examination) must be standing bodies. In reality, Select and Joint Committees are classic Ad Hoc committees — they are constituted for one specific Bill and cease to exist upon submitting their report.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary committees are broadly classified as Standing (permanent, reconstituted periodically) and Ad Hoc (temporary, dissolving upon completing their specific task). The basis of constitution also differs: Standing Committees are created under the Rules of Procedure, while Ad Hoc Committees are constituted by special motion or order for a specific purpose.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Select Committees are Ad Hoc, not Standing. They are formed for a specific Bill and dissolve after reporting.
• Option (b) — Correct: A Joint Committee of both Houses on a Bill is a classic Ad Hoc committee — it dissolves after presenting its report.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Public Accounts Committee is a Financial Standing Committee, not Ad Hoc.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Business Advisory Committee is a Standing Committee constituted under Rules of Procedure.

Value Addition:
• Standing Committees include Financial Committees (PAC, Estimates, CPU), DRSCs, and procedural committees (BAC, Rules, Privileges, Ethics).
• Ad Hoc Committees include Select Committees, Joint Committees on Bills, and Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs).
• The key test: if a committee dissolves after fulfilling its purpose, it is Ad Hoc.

solution.concept_anchor: Estimates Committee composition and PAC orientation

statement_analysis.statement: The Estimates Committee consists entirely of members drawn from Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha has no representation in it.
statement_analysis.reason: The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all elected from Lok Sabha. Unlike other financial committees, Rajya Sabha members have no seat in it — this is a unique structural feature.

statement_analysis.statement: The Public Accounts Committee examines government expenditure with a forward-looking perspective to suggest economies before funds are spent.
statement_analysis.reason: PAC is retrospective in nature — it examines post-expenditure accounts and CAG audit reports to assess whether money was spent as Parliament sanctioned. Forward-looking economy suggestions are the domain of the Estimates Committee.

statement_analysis.statement: The Estimates Committee's recommendations regarding government estimates are advisory and not binding on the executive.
statement_analysis.reason: The Estimates Committee can suggest economies and improvements in organisation, but its recommendations do not compel the government to alter estimates — they are persuasive, not mandatory.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Selecting all three statements feels correct to students who conflate the forward-looking function of the Estimates Committee with the PAC's described role, missing that Statement 2 has reversed the orientation of PAC.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Estimates Committee is exclusively a Lok Sabha committee with 30 members — Rajya Sabha has no representation. Statement 1 is Correct.

Verify Statement 2: PAC examines post-expenditure accounts (backward-looking), not pre-expenditure estimates. Statement 2 incorrectly attributes a forward-looking role to PAC. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Estimates Committee recommendations are advisory and non-binding on the government. Statement 3 is Correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the common confusion between the PAC and the Estimates Committee. Both deal with government finances, but they differ fundamentally in temporal orientation: the Estimates Committee is prospective (examines estimates before spending), while PAC is retrospective (audits post-expenditure accounts). A student who vaguely remembers 'financial committees suggest economies' may tick Statement 2 as correct, selecting option (d). Precise knowledge of the directional difference separates the prepared candidate.
solution.final_explanation:
India's three financial committees — Estimates Committee, PAC, and CPU — each occupy a distinct niche in parliamentary financial oversight. Their composition, scope, and temporal orientation differ sharply.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from Lok Sabha. Rajya Sabha has no representation, making it unique among the three financial committees. This is because money Bills originate in Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha has no direct role in their passage.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: PAC is inherently backward-looking. It scrutinises how money was spent against parliamentary sanction, using CAG audit reports as its primary input. Pre-expenditure economy suggestions belong to the Estimates Committee.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Estimates Committee recommendations are persuasive, not binding. The government may accept, modify, or ignore them — Parliament cannot compel the executive through committee recommendations.

Value Addition:
• PAC has 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS); the Leader of Opposition from LS chairs it by convention since 1967.
• CPU has 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS) and focuses on PSUs, not ministries.
• All three financial committees examine CAG reports in some capacity, but only PAC and CPU have Rajya Sabha representation.

solution.concept_anchor: PAC role and chairperson convention

statement_analysis.statement: The convention of the Leader of Opposition chairing the Public Accounts Committee is a constitutionally mandated requirement.
statement_analysis.reason: The convention of the Leader of Opposition from Lok Sabha chairing the PAC dates to 1967 but is a convention, not a constitutional or statutory requirement. It is not mentioned in any rule or constitutional provision.

statement_analysis.statement: The Public Accounts Committee can hold the executive accountable for departures from government policy when appropriating funds.
statement_analysis.reason: PAC does not question policy decisions per se. It examines whether funds were spent as Parliament intended — within the sanctioned appropriation — not whether the underlying policy was correct. Policy scrutiny is beyond its remit.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) (Statement 2 only is incorrect) tempts students who know Statement 1 is a convention and mistakenly classify 'convention' as still constitutionally valid, while correctly identifying Statement 2 as wrong.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: The LoP chairing PAC is a convention from 1967, not a constitutional provision or rule of procedure. Statement 1 is Incorrect.

Verify Statement 2: PAC examines compliance with parliamentary appropriation, not the merit of policy. Holding executives accountable for policy departures is not its function. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Both statements are incorrect — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits confusion between conventions and constitutional mandates. Students aware that the Leader of Opposition chairs the PAC may assume it is legally required rather than a political convention. Statement 2 exploits the partial truth that PAC does hold the executive accountable — but only for financial irregularities against parliamentary sanction, not for policy choices. Together, both statements feel plausible at a surface level.
solution.final_explanation:
The PAC is the oldest and most prominent of India's financial committees, tracing its origins to 1921. Its precise mandate and the conventions surrounding it are frequently tested.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The LoP from Lok Sabha chairing the PAC is a political convention established in 1967, not a constitutional or statutory requirement. It reflects the democratic principle that financial oversight should be led by the opposition, but no rule compels it.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: PAC scrutinises post-expenditure accounts against parliamentary appropriation. It checks whether money was spent as Parliament intended, within sanctioned heads. It cannot and does not question whether the underlying policy was sound — that is Parliament's prerogative on the floor.

Value Addition:
• PAC has 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha. It is a joint committee for the financial year.
• The CAG's report (submitted under Article 151) is the primary document examined by PAC — CAG is often called the 'friend, philosopher and guide' of PAC.
• PAC's retrospective nature distinguishes it from the Estimates Committee, which examines estimates prospectively.

solution.concept_anchor: CPU scope exclusions and composition accuracy

statement_analysis.statement: The Committee on Public Undertakings has 22 members, with 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: CPU has exactly 22 members — 15 elected from Lok Sabha and 7 elected from Rajya Sabha — the same total as PAC but with an identical composition ratio.

statement_analysis.statement: The Committee on Public Undertakings can examine the working of PSUs engaged in defence production to assess financial efficiency.
statement_analysis.reason: CPU explicitly excludes PSUs engaged in defence, atomic energy, and matters involving national security considerations from its scope of examination.

statement_analysis.statement: The Committee on Public Undertakings scrutinises CAG reports on public sector undertakings.
statement_analysis.reason: One of CPU's primary functions is to examine CAG audit reports relating to PSUs, similar to how PAC examines CAG reports on government ministries.

statement_analysis.statement: The Committee on Public Undertakings can review matters of major government policy as it pertains to public undertakings.
statement_analysis.reason: CPU cannot examine matters of major government policy or day-to-day administration of PSUs. It is restricted to examining whether PSUs are managed efficiently within existing policy.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 but mistakenly believe defence PSUs fall within CPU's scope given its broad mandate over 'public undertakings.'
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: CPU has 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS) — this is accurate. Statement 1 is Correct.
Verify Statement 2: CPU is barred from examining defence and atomic energy PSUs due to security considerations. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: CPU examines CAG reports on PSUs — this is a core function. Statement 3 is Correct.
Verify Statement 4: CPU cannot examine major policy matters or day-to-day administration of PSUs. Statement 4 is Incorrect.
Only two statements (1 and 3) are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the assumption that a committee examining 'public undertakings' has unlimited scope over all government-owned enterprises. Defence PSUs are explicitly excluded from CPU's examination — a nuance most students miss. Statement 4 exploits the assumption that if CPU can scrutinise PSU finances, it must also be able to question policy — another misconception. Policy review is left to Parliament itself.
solution.final_explanation:
The Committee on Public Undertakings occupies a specific niche: it bridges financial oversight (like PAC) with administrative review of government-owned enterprises. However, its scope has important exclusions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: CPU has 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS), mirroring PAC in composition size.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: PSUs in defence, atomic energy, and national security sectors are beyond CPU's examination. These exclusions protect sensitive operational information.
• Statement 3 — Correct: CPU examines CAG audit reports on PSUs — this is its primary evidentiary input, similar to PAC's use of CAG reports for ministries.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: CPU cannot examine major government policy. It can only assess whether PSUs operate efficiently within the policy framework already set.

Value Addition:
• CPU was constituted in 1964 — it is the youngest of the three financial committees.
• PAC examines government ministries; CPU examines PSUs — both use CAG reports as their primary tool.
• The Estimates Committee is the only financial committee with no Rajya Sabha representation.

solution.concept_anchor: Financial committee composition and orientation comparison

elimination_logic: Anchor on the unambiguous pair: Estimates Committee — 30 members, all from Lok Sabha only. This confirms A matches 3.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in the CPU-PAC conflation. Both have 22 members and both examine CAG reports, but CPU focuses on PSUs while PAC focuses on government ministries. Students who remember '22 members + CAG reports' may assign both descriptions interchangeably. The DRSC description (31 members, both Houses, ministry-specific) is the anchor that helps eliminate wrong combinations if remembered precisely.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precise knowledge of committee-specific attributes across four major parliamentary committees.

Correct pairings:

Trap pairing: B and C both involve 22 members and CAG reports — the distinction is PSUs (CPU) vs government ministries (PAC).

Value Addition:
• DRSCs were originally 17 in 1993, expanded to 24 in 2004.
• Only the Estimates Committee excludes Rajya Sabha — a constitutional design reflecting Rajya Sabha's limited role in money matters.
• PAC's retrospective and CPU's PSU focus are classic UPSC pairing traps.

solution.concept_anchor: Money Bills cannot be referred to Joint Committee
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both A and R are correct but do not think carefully about whether R actually explains A may select (a), missing that R is factually incorrect.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Money Bills cannot be referred to a Joint Committee of both Houses. This is established practice and flows from the special constitutional position of Money Bills under Article 110.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. The reason stated — that Joint Committees have no power to summon witnesses — is factually wrong. Joint Committees do have powers to summon witnesses and call for papers, which is precisely why they are useful for Bill scrutiny.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer must be option (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap operates on two levels. First, students who know that Money Bills are constitutionally protected may assume any reason connected to that protection must be correct. Second, students with vague knowledge of Joint Committees may not know whether they possess summons powers — making the false R appear plausible. The actual reason Money Bills cannot be referred to a Joint Committee is their special constitutional status (requiring only Lok Sabha's ultimate approval), not any limitation on the committee's powers.
solution.final_explanation:
Assertion (A) is constitutionally accurate: Money Bills, as defined under Article 110, cannot be referred to a Joint Committee of both Houses. This flows from their special status — they require Rajya Sabha's agreement only on Lok Sabha's terms.

Reason (R) is factually wrong: Joint Committees on Bills do possess quasi-judicial powers — they can summon witnesses (including experts and officials), examine evidence, and call for documents. The absence of these powers would make them ineffective for scrutinising complex legislation.

The correct explanation for why Money Bills cannot go to a Joint Committee is that such referral would give Rajya Sabha equal standing in examining and recommending changes to a Money Bill, undermining the constitutional primacy of Lok Sabha in financial legislation.

Value Addition:
• Select Committee = members of one House only; Joint Committee = members of both Houses — the key structural distinction.
• Ordinary Bills can be referred to either a Select Committee or a Joint Committee.
• Both are Ad Hoc — they dissolve after presenting their report.
• Constitution Bills (Amendment Bills under Article 368) are also not typically referred to Joint Committees.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

Role of DRSCs in Pre-legislative Scrutiny vs Post-legislative Review

solution.concept_anchor: DRSC Bill referral is discretionary, not mandatory
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know DRSCs examine Bills may assume the government must refer a Bill to the relevant DRSC, making option (a) seem constitutionally required.
elimination_logic: Identify the core legal issue: Is referral of a Bill to a DRSC mandatory or discretionary?
Eliminate option (a): Referral of a Bill to a DRSC is not mandatory under any constitutional provision or rule — it is at the discretion of the Speaker/Chairman or the House.
Eliminate option (c): A DRSC cannot itself claim jurisdiction over a Bill — it has no power to demand referral of pending legislation.
Eliminate option (d): DRSCs are not restricted to only post-passage review — they can examine Bills before passage (pre-legislative scrutiny).
Select option (b): The Speaker/Chairman has the discretion to refer the Bill to the relevant DRSC, but the government is not compelled to do so.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This scenario exploits the widespread but incorrect belief that important Bills must go through DRSC scrutiny. In practice, major legislation such as the Citizenship Amendment Act, the three Farm Laws, and several labour codes bypassed DRSC examination entirely. The constitutional and procedural reality is that referral is discretionary — vested in the Speaker or Chairman. Many civil society and parliamentary reform advocates have argued for making referral mandatory, but no such rule exists.
solution.final_explanation:
DRSCs were designed to conduct detailed legislative scrutiny that is impossible on the crowded floor of the House. Their pre-legislative function — examining Bills clause by clause — is one of their most valued but underutilised roles.

However, reference of a Bill to a DRSC is not mandatory. Under the Rules of Procedure, the Speaker (Lok Sabha) or Chairman (Rajya Sabha) may refer a Bill to the relevant DRSC, or the House itself may pass a motion to do so. The executive is not compelled to route legislation through committee scrutiny.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No rule or constitutional provision mandates referral of Bills to DRSCs.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Speaker/Chairman exercises discretion. The organisation can only advocate, not compel, DRSC scrutiny.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: DRSCs have no inherent power to claim jurisdiction over pending Bills.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: DRSCs can examine Bills both before and after passage, and also examine annual reports and demands for grants.

Value Addition:
• PRS Legislative Research has documented a declining trend in Bills referred to DRSCs in recent years.
• Second ARC and parliamentary reform debates have recommended mandatory DRSC referral for all non-financial Bills.
• DRSCs cover 24 ministry clusters (post-2004 expansion), each committee having 31 members from both Houses.

solution.concept_anchor: Subordinate legislation committee scope vs papers committee
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may select the Committee on Papers Laid on the Table as the odd one out because it sounds administrative, missing that it too is a scrutiny committee focused on procedural compliance.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: Three of the four options relate to committees that scrutinise delegated or subordinate forms of executive action/legislation.
Committee on Subordinate Legislation — scrutinises rules and regulations framed under delegated authority. Fits the scrutiny theme.
Committee on Papers Laid on the Table — scrutinises procedural compliance in laying statutory documents. Fits the scrutiny theme.
Committee on Government Assurances — scrutinises ministerial promises made on the floor of the House. Fits the scrutiny/accountability theme.
The Library Committee — supervises the Parliamentary Library and assists members in research. It has no scrutiny, accountability, or legislative oversight function. It is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Library Committee sounds parliamentary and therefore 'legislative' to a casual reader. Students who do not know its purely administrative/housekeeping function may confuse it with substantive scrutiny committees. The three other options all perform an oversight or accountability role over executive actions — scrutinising delegated legislation, statutory documents, and ministerial assurances respectively. The Library Committee performs none of these functions.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary committees serve diverse functions: some scrutinise legislation, some oversee finances, and some are purely administrative. Distinguishing these categories is essential.

• Option (a) — Committee on Subordinate Legislation: Examines rules, regulations, and bye-laws framed under delegated authority — a substantive oversight function.
• Option (b) — Committee on Papers Laid on the Table: Examines whether documents tabled by Ministers meet procedural requirements under statute — a procedural oversight function.
• Option (c) — Library Committee: Supervises the Parliamentary Library; assists members with research. It has zero legislative, financial, or accountability oversight role — purely administrative/housekeeping.
• Option (d) — Committee on Government Assurances: Tracks whether ministerial promises made on the floor are fulfilled — a direct accountability function.

Value Addition:
• Library Committee and House Committee (residential amenities) are classified as 'service committees' — not scrutiny bodies.
• Both Houses have separate Committees on Subordinate Legislation — they are not joint committees.
• Committee on Papers Laid on the Table scrutinises procedural compliance only — it does not assess the merits of the documents tabled.

solution.concept_anchor: BAC vs Rules Committee function distinction

statement_analysis.statement: The Business Advisory Committee recommends amendments to the Rules of Procedure of the respective House.
statement_analysis.reason: Recommending amendments to Rules of Procedure is the function of the Rules Committee, not the Business Advisory Committee. The BAC's function is to recommend allocation of time for legislative and other business in the House.

statement_analysis.statement: Both the Business Advisory Committee and the Rules Committee in Lok Sabha are chaired by the Speaker.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker chairs both the Business Advisory Committee and the Rules Committee in Lok Sabha. In Rajya Sabha, the Chairman chairs the equivalent bodies. This makes them unique among parliamentary committees where a non-member presides.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Wait: the correct answer IS (a). The distractor here is option (c), which tempts students who correctly identify Statement 2 as true but incorrectly believe Statement 1 is also true, selecting option (a) prematurely without verifying Statement 1.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: BAC allocates time for business; it does NOT recommend amendments to Rules of Procedure. That is the Rules Committee's function. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 2: Speaker chairs both BAC and Rules Committee in Lok Sabha — this is accurate. Statement 2 is Correct.
Statement 1 Incorrect + Statement 2 Correct = option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The BAC and Rules Committee are both chaired by the Speaker and deal with procedural aspects of Parliament, creating conflation risk. Students who know both are 'procedural' committees may attribute the Rules Committee's function (amending Rules of Procedure) to the BAC. The distinction is: BAC schedules business (what gets discussed and when); Rules Committee changes the framework within which business is conducted (the procedural rules themselves).
solution.final_explanation:
The BAC and Rules Committee are both Speaker-chaired bodies dealing with parliamentary procedure, but their mandates are sharply distinct.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: BAC recommends the allocation of time for government business and other legislative items on the House's agenda. Amendments to the Rules of Procedure fall within the Rules Committee's domain — not BAC's.
• Statement 2 — Correct: In Lok Sabha, the Speaker chairs both the BAC and the Rules Committee. Similarly, the Rajya Sabha Chairman chairs the corresponding bodies. This is a notable feature — the presiding officer leads both procedural management committees.

Value Addition:
• BAC recommendations on time allocation are advisory — the Speaker retains final authority on scheduling.
• Rules Committee recommendations on procedural amendments must be approved by the full House before taking effect.
• BAC includes leaders of recognised parties and groups — its composition reflects the political balance of the House.

solution.concept_anchor: Ethics Committee establishment timeline RS vs LS
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) reverses the order (Lok Sabha 1997, Rajya Sabha 2000), which feels plausible since Lok Sabha is the more prominent House and students may assume it acted first.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Ethics Committee is not constitutionally mandated — this is a key fact distinguishing it from many other committees.
Eliminate option (c): Rajya Sabha established its Ethics Committee in 1997, before Lok Sabha (2000) — not the other way around.
Eliminate option (d): 1990/1995 are fabricated years — neither House established an Ethics Committee in the 1990s before 1997.
Select option (b): Rajya Sabha (1997) preceded Lok Sabha (2000) — the correct order.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students instinctively assume Lok Sabha acts before Rajya Sabha on most institutional reforms since it is the primary chamber. In this case, the Rajya Sabha was the pioneer — it established the Ethics Committee in 1997, three years before Lok Sabha did so in 2000. Option (c) exploits this assumption by reversing the order. Additionally, many students confuse the Ethics Committee with the Privileges Committee, conflating moral/professional accountability with legal breach-of-privilege proceedings.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ethics Committee is a relatively recent addition to the parliamentary committee system, distinct from the longer-established Privileges Committee.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Ethics Committee is not constitutionally mandated. It was created through procedural rules, not a constitutional provision — unlike, say, the PAC whose basis lies in rules connected to Article 151.
• Option (b) — Correct: Rajya Sabha established its Ethics Committee in 1997; Lok Sabha followed in 2000.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: This reverses the chronology. Rajya Sabha was the pioneer, not Lok Sabha.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Neither House established an Ethics Committee before 1997.

Value Addition:
• Privileges Committee handles breach of legal rights of the House; Ethics Committee deals with moral/professional misconduct of members.
• Ethics Committee recommendations are not automatically binding — the full House retains final authority.
• The Privileges Committee can recommend punishments including reprimand, suspension, or expulsion.

solution.concept_anchor: JPC findings are recommendatory, not judicially enforceable
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) appeals to students who know JPCs have wide powers (summoning ministers and officials) and assume these translate into enforceable directives.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): JPC is constituted by a motion passed in one House and concurred by the other — not by an executive order.
Eliminate option (b): JPC can summon ministers and officials — it is not restricted to only examining documents.
Eliminate option (d): JPC findings are presented to Parliament as a report — they are recommendatory and not judicially enforceable. Courts are not bound by JPC conclusions.
Select option (c): JPC is an Ad Hoc committee — it dissolves after presenting its report to Parliament.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The JPC's high political profile (Bofors, Harshad Mehta scam, 2G spectrum) leads students to overestimate its legal authority. Because it can summon senior officials and ministers, students assume its findings carry judicial or executive force. In reality, JPC findings are recommendatory — they are tabled in Parliament as a report and carry political but not legal enforceability. Courts have separately prosecuted individuals in cases where JPCs have also reported, but the JPC itself has no prosecutorial or enforcement authority.
solution.final_explanation:
Joint Parliamentary Committees investigating specific matters of public importance are classic Ad Hoc committees with high political significance but limited formal legal power.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: A JPC is constituted when one House passes a motion and the other House concurs — it is a parliamentary, not executive, creation.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: JPCs can summon witnesses including ministers, officials, and experts. They are not limited to documentary examination.
• Option (c) — Correct: JPCs are Ad Hoc — they are constituted for a specific inquiry and dissolve upon presenting their report to Parliament.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: JPC findings are recommendatory. They are tabled as a report in Parliament. Courts are not bound by JPC conclusions, and any criminal prosecution follows from judicial processes, not JPC orders.

Value Addition:
• Notable JPCs: Bofors (1987), Harshad Mehta securities scam (1992), 2G spectrum allocation (2011).
• JPC differs from a Select/Joint Committee on a Bill — JPCs investigate matters, not legislation.
• The political significance of a JPC is often disproportionate to its formal legal powers.

solution.concept_anchor: Government Assurances committee scope exclusions

statement_analysis.statement: The Committee on Government Assurances in each House scrutinises only the assurances made by Ministers on the floor of that respective House — it does not cover assurances given in the other House.
statement_analysis.reason: Separate Committees on Government Assurances exist in each House, and each covers only assurances made on the floor of its own House during Question Hour, debates, and other proceedings.

statement_analysis.statement: The Committee on Government Assurances examines policy commitments made by the Finance Minister in Budget speeches to track their implementation.
statement_analysis.reason: Budget speech commitments are not 'assurances' under this committee's jurisdiction. The committee covers only assurances made during floor proceedings such as Question Hour and debates — not Budget or policy documents.

statement_analysis.statement: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation can examine the parent Act under which delegated powers have been granted to assess whether the delegation itself was appropriate.
statement_analysis.reason: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation examines only the rules, regulations, and notifications framed under delegated authority — not the parent Act itself. Whether the delegation was appropriate is a matter for Parliament when enacting the parent legislation.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Selecting all three as correct is the most dangerous error: Statement 2 sounds perfectly reasonable (Budget commitments are ministerial), and Statement 3 sounds logical (why wouldn't the committee look at the source of power?).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Each House has its own Committee on Government Assurances covering only its own floor proceedings. Statement 1 is Correct.
Verify Statement 2: Budget speech commitments are not within scope — only floor assurances during Question Hour, debates etc. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Committee on Subordinate Legislation examines rules framed under the parent Act, not the Act itself. Statement 3 is Incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the logical assumption that if a committee tracks ministerial promises, Budget commitments must be the most important such promises to track. The committee's scope is narrower — it covers only oral and written assurances during floor proceedings. Statement 3 exploits the idea that examining delegated legislation should naturally include the source of that delegation. The committee's mandate is deliberately narrow: it only checks compliance within the delegation, not the delegation's wisdom.
solution.final_explanation:
Both the Committee on Government Assurances and the Committee on Subordinate Legislation have carefully circumscribed mandates that are commonly misunderstood.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Separate committees in each House cover only floor assurances of that House. There is no cross-House jurisdiction.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Budget speeches, policy documents, and electoral promises are outside the committee's scope. Only assurances made during Question Hour, debates, Private Member's Bills discussions, etc., are covered.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation scrutinises whether rules/regulations stay within the scope of delegation granted by the parent Act — it does not revisit or evaluate the parent Act itself.

Value Addition:
• Committee on Government Assurances checks implementation timeliness — it tracks 'pending assurances' that remain unfulfilled.
• Committee on Subordinate Legislation is a Standing Committee but is separate in each House — not a joint committee.
• Committee on Papers Laid on the Table is the closest counterpart — it checks procedural compliance in tabling documents, not their substance.

solution.concept_anchor: Committee quorum and secrecy of proceedings

statement_analysis.statement: The quorum for a meeting of any parliamentary committee is one-half of its total membership.
statement_analysis.reason: The quorum for parliamentary committees is one-third of total membership, not one-half. One-half is the quorum requirement for the full House.

statement_analysis.statement: A Minister who is a member of a Departmentally Related Standing Committee cannot participate in that committee's examination of the Demands for Grants of their own ministry.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a deliberate procedural safeguard: a Minister sitting in a DRSC cannot participate when their own ministry's Demands for Grants are being examined — to prevent conflict of interest and ensure independent scrutiny.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliamentary committees can meet only during parliamentary sessions and not during inter-session periods.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliamentary committees, including DRSCs, can and regularly do meet during inter-session periods. This is one of their key advantages over full House proceedings, which require a session to be in progress.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students selecting option (c) (only Statement 3 is incorrect) correctly identify the inter-session meeting issue but miss that the one-half quorum figure in Statement 1 is also wrong.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Quorum for committees is one-third of membership, not one-half. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 2: A Minister cannot participate in DRSC scrutiny of their own ministry's grants — this is a genuine procedural rule. Statement 2 is Correct.
Verify Statement 3: Committees routinely meet during inter-session periods — this is a key procedural feature. Statement 3 is Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the tendency to apply full-House quorum rules to committees. The House requires one-half; committees require only one-third. Statement 3 exploits the instinct that parliamentary bodies can function only when Parliament is in session. Committees are specifically designed to work between sessions — this continuity is central to their value. Both traps use 'reasonable-sounding' substitutions that feel correct without precise knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary committees have distinct procedural rules that differ significantly from those governing the full House.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Committee quorum is one-third of total membership. The one-half requirement applies to the full House (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Many students conflate these.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The rule preventing a Minister from participating in DRSC scrutiny of their own ministry is a critical conflict-of-interest safeguard. It ensures the scrutiny function remains independent.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Parliamentary committees regularly meet during inter-session periods. In fact, the ability to work continuously — unlike the full House — is one of the strongest arguments for the committee system.

Value Addition:
• Committee proceedings are secret — members cannot disclose evidence or deliberations before the report is presented to the House.
• Committees can take evidence from experts, administrators, and civil society, making them effective technical scrutiny bodies.
• DRSCs meet an average of 20–30 times per year, including inter-session sittings.

solution.concept_anchor: DRSC evolution 1993 to 2004 expansion
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places the 24-committee expansion before the 17-committee origin, which appeals to students who remember '24' as the number and vaguely recall the 1993 reform without knowing which number came first.
elimination_logic: Anchor on the founding event: DRSCs were originally constituted with 17 committees in 1993 — this is the starting point.
The expansion to 24 committees occurred in 2004 — this came after the 1993 origin.
Eliminate options placing the 24-committee phase before the 17-committee phase.
The correct sequence is: 17 committees (1993) → 24 committees (2004). Select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who remember DRSCs as '24 committees' may place the 2004 expansion first, especially if they recall it as the 'current' structure and treat 1993 as a later refinement. The trap is temporal: '24' is the more familiar number because it is the post-2004 figure that appears in most textbooks. Knowing that DRSCs started with 17 committees in 1993 and were expanded to 24 in 2004 requires chronological precision, not just factual recall.
solution.final_explanation:
The DRSC system has evolved through distinct phases since its introduction as a mechanism for detailed legislative and budgetary scrutiny.

Correct sequence:
1. 1993 — DRSCs were first constituted with 17 committees covering various ministry clusters. This marked a significant reform in parliamentary oversight.
2. 2004 — The system was expanded to 24 committees to cover all central government ministries and departments more comprehensively.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (b): Placing the 24-committee expansion before the 1993 origin reverses the chronology.
• Option (c): Placing the expansion in 1998 is a temporal fabrication — no such expansion occurred then.
• Option (d): Swapping the years (2004 as origin, 1993 as expansion) is internally illogical.

Value Addition:
• Each DRSC has 31 members drawn from both Houses (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha).
• DRSCs are reconstituted annually and can examine Bills, Demands for Grants, and annual reports.
• Recent proposals (2024 context) have discussed restructuring DRSCs to 8 broader clusters, though no final restructuring has been adopted.

solution.concept_anchor: Privileges Committee recommends; House decides final order
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both A and R are correct and see a surface connection between 'investigation' and 'passing final judgment' may select (a), missing that R does not causally explain A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Committee on Privileges investigates and recommends; it is the full House that passes the final order on breach of privilege. This is an established procedural fact.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. R claims that the Privileges Committee is constitutionally constituted under a specific provision of the Constitution. In fact, the Committee on Privileges is constituted under the Rules of Procedure — it has no direct constitutional basis in a specific article. (Parliamentary privileges as such are under Articles 105/194, but the committee itself is a creature of rules.)
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer is option (c): A is correct, R is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap operates by invoking the correct fact that parliamentary privileges are constitutionally protected (Articles 105, 194) and then falsely attributing the Privileges Committee's constitution to a specific constitutional article. Students who know privileges are constitutional rights may assume the committee enforcing them is also directly constitutionally created. In reality, the committee is constituted under Rules of Procedure — the constitutional protection applies to the privileges themselves, not to the committee mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
The Committee on Privileges occupies a quasi-judicial role in maintaining the dignity and independence of Parliament, but its procedural limits are precisely defined.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The Privileges Committee only investigates allegations of breach of privilege and makes recommendations (including reprimand, suspension, or expulsion). The House itself, through a resolution or order, takes the final action. The committee cannot independently impose punishment.

Reason (R) — Incorrect: The Committee on Privileges is constituted under the Rules of Procedure of the respective House — not under a specific constitutional article. Parliamentary privileges themselves are protected under Articles 105 (Parliament) and 194 (State Legislatures), but the committee mechanism is a rules-based creation.

Since A is correct and R is incorrect, the answer is option (c).

Value Addition:
• The Speaker nominates members of the Privileges Committee and chairs it (in Lok Sabha) ex officio without being a formal member.
• Breach of privilege can arise from actions both inside and outside the House that obstruct members in discharge of their duties.
• The Ethics Committee deals with moral/professional misconduct — distinct from the legal/rights-based jurisdiction of the Privileges Committee.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

solution.concept_anchor: Consultative Committees not parliamentary committees; no formal powers
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) claims Consultative Committees can examine annual reports of ministries, which sounds plausible because DRSCs do so — students may conflate the two.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Consultative Committees are constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, not by the Lok Sabha Rules Committee — a fabrication.
Eliminate option (b): Consultative Committees cannot examine annual reports in a formal capacity — that is a DRSC function. Consultative Committees only provide an informal discussion forum.
Eliminate option (c): Consultative Committees cannot summon witnesses — this is a formal power available only to DRSCs, Select/Joint Committees, and financial committees.

Select option (d): Consultative Committees are constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs and provide only an informal forum for discussion — they have no formal powers. This pair is correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Options (b) and (c) deliberately borrow functions from DRSCs and apply them to Consultative Committees. Students who confuse Consultative Committees with DRSCs may select these. The critical distinction: Consultative Committees have no formal powers whatsoever — no summons authority, no formal document examination, no report submission to Parliament. They exist solely for informal dialogue between Ministers and MPs about ministry policies.
solution.final_explanation:
Consultative Committees are frequently confused with parliamentary committees, especially DRSCs, because both involve MPs discussing ministry policies.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Consultative Committees are constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, not by the Rules Committee — fabricated attribution.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Formal examination of ministry annual reports belongs to DRSCs, not Consultative Committees, which have no such formal mandate.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Consultative Committees cannot summon witnesses or call for papers — they have no formal powers of any kind.
• Option (d) — Correct: Constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs; provide only an informal dialogue forum between Ministers and MPs; no formal powers.

Value Addition:
• Consultative Committees meet both during sessions and inter-session periods — membership is voluntary for MPs.
• They are not parliamentary committees in the strict legal sense — their proceedings are not recorded as formal parliamentary proceedings.
• DRSCs are the formal counterpart to Consultative Committees — with binding examination powers (though non-binding recommendations).

solution.concept_anchor: SC/ST Welfare Committee scope and Library Committee nature

statement_analysis.statement: The Joint Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes can examine the working of constitutional safeguards such as reservation provisions in both Union and State governments.
statement_analysis.reason: The committee's mandate extends to examining welfare measures and the implementation of constitutional safeguards (Articles 17, 46, reservations) in both Union and State government contexts.

statement_analysis.statement: The Joint Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes can override state legislation that is found to be inadequate in protecting the rights of SCs and STs.
statement_analysis.reason: The committee is strictly a recommendatory body with no executive authority. It cannot override, repeal, or invalidate state legislation — that power rests with Parliament or the courts.

statement_analysis.statement: The Library Committee of Parliament is a joint committee that assists members in legislative research and supervises the Parliamentary Library — it has no legislative scrutiny role.
statement_analysis.reason: The Library Committee is a housekeeping/service committee. It supervises the Parliamentary Library and assists members with information and research needs — it performs no legislative, financial, or accountability scrutiny function.

statement_analysis.statement: The House Committee of Parliament oversees residential accommodation and amenities for members, and its decisions on accommodation are binding on the government.
statement_analysis.reason: The House Committee looks after residential accommodation for members, but it functions as an administrative body making recommendations — its decisions are not described as binding directives overriding executive discretion.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may select three as correct by including Statement 4, reasoning that a parliamentary committee dealing with member housing would naturally have its decisions respected as binding.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: SC/ST Welfare Committee examines constitutional safeguards in Union and State contexts. Statement 1 is Correct.
Verify Statement 2: The committee is recommendatory only — it cannot override state legislation. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Library Committee supervises the library and assists members — pure service function, no scrutiny role. Statement 3 is Correct.
Verify Statement 4: House Committee handles accommodation; binding authority over government is overstated. Statement 4 is Incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the assumption that a committee examining constitutional safeguards must have constitutional enforcement powers. It does not — recommendatory bodies cannot invalidate or override legislation regardless of their subject matter. Statement 4 exploits the assumption that administrative decisions by parliamentary committees are automatically binding — they are not. All parliamentary committee recommendations, whether on legislation or internal administration, require executive or House action to take effect.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary committees dealing with specific constituencies (SC/ST, women) and internal administration (Library, House) operate at very different levels but share one common feature: their recommendations are not self-executing.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The SC/ST Welfare Committee examines Union and State government measures implementing constitutional safeguards for SCs and STs.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The committee is purely recommendatory — it has no power to override state legislation. Only Parliament or the judiciary can invalidate state laws.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Library Committee is a joint service committee focused on the Parliamentary Library — it performs no legislative, financial, or oversight function.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The House Committee makes recommendations on member accommodation — it does not issue binding directives to the government.

Value Addition:
• Committee on Empowerment of Women has a similar mandate to the SC/ST Welfare Committee but focuses on legislation and policies affecting women.
• Library Committee, House Committee, and similar bodies are classified as 'housekeeping' or 'service' committees.
• All parliamentary committees — regardless of subject — can only recommend; final authority rests with the House or the executive.

solution.concept_anchor: Declining Bill referrals and non-binding recommendations critique

statement_analysis.statement: Parliamentary committee recommendations on Bills are not binding on the government, meaning the executive can choose not to accept any amendments suggested by the committee.
statement_analysis.reason: All parliamentary committee recommendations — including those of DRSCs on Bills — are advisory. The government is not legally obligated to accept or incorporate any amendment suggested by a committee.

statement_analysis.statement: The bypassing of DRSC scrutiny for major legislation in India is constitutionally prohibited, and such Bills must be referred to a DRSC before being put to vote.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no constitutional prohibition on bypassing DRSC scrutiny. Reference to DRSCs is discretionary — vested in the Speaker or Chairman. Several major Bills have been passed without DRSC referral, and this practice is not unconstitutional.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify Statement 1 as true may assume Statement 2 is also true because bypassing committee scrutiny 'should' be unconstitutional given the importance of oversight — a normative rather than legal reasoning error.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Committee recommendations are advisory, not binding. The executive retains full discretion. Statement 1 is Correct.
Verify Statement 2: No constitutional provision prohibits bypassing DRSC scrutiny. Major legislation has regularly bypassed committees without constitutional challenge. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 1 Correct + Statement 2 Incorrect = option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the normative expectation that an important oversight mechanism should be mandatory. Students who believe that bypassing committee scrutiny is problematic may assume it must therefore be prohibited. The distinction between 'normatively desirable' and 'legally required' is the trap. DRSC referral is discretionary — reform advocates argue it should be mandatory, but it currently is not.
solution.final_explanation:
The parliamentary committee system's effectiveness is fundamentally constrained by the non-binding nature of its recommendations and the discretionary referral mechanism.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Committee recommendations — whether on Bills, budgets, or policies — are advisory. The executive can accept, modify, or ignore them without any legal consequence.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No constitutional provision mandates referral of Bills to DRSCs. The Speaker or Chairman exercises discretionary authority. Bills like the Citizenship Amendment Act, Farm Laws, and several labour codes were passed without DRSC referral — a practice criticised but not unconstitutional.

Value Addition:
• PRS Legislative Research has documented a sharp decline in Bills referred to DRSCs since 2014.
• Second Administrative Reforms Commission and various parliamentary reform advocates have recommended mandatory referral of all non-financial Bills to DRSCs.
• UK Select Committees have stronger influence; US Congressional Committees are central to legislation — India's committee system is relatively weaker in comparison.

Select Committee and Joint Committee on Bills: Nature and Powers

solution.concept_anchor: Ad Hoc committee types and their dissolution triggers

statement_analysis.statement: A Select Committee constituted to examine a specific Bill consists of members from both Houses of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: A Select Committee consists of members of one House only. A committee with members from both Houses examining a Bill is called a Joint Committee, not a Select Committee.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Select Committees and Joint Parliamentary Committees investigating specific matters dissolve after presenting their respective reports.
statement_analysis.reason: Both are classic Ad Hoc committees — their existence is tied to a specific purpose (a Bill or an investigation). Upon presenting the report to Parliament, they stand dissolved.

statement_analysis.statement: A Joint Parliamentary Committee investigating a financial scam can summon Ministers and senior officials to record evidence.
statement_analysis.reason: JPCs have the power to summon witnesses, including Ministers and senior officials, and to examine documents — making them effective investigative bodies, though their findings remain recommendatory.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Selecting all three is the strongest trap: Statement 1 uses the word 'Select Committee' but describes a Joint Committee, and the difference between the two is frequently blurred by students.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Select Committee = one House only. Members from both Houses = Joint Committee. Statement 1 describes a Joint Committee but calls it a Select Committee. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 2: Both Select Committees and JPCs are Ad Hoc and dissolve after presenting reports. Statement 2 is Correct.
Verify Statement 3: JPCs can summon witnesses including Ministers — this is an established power. Statement 3 is Correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is the primary trap: it correctly describes a Joint Committee (members from both Houses examining a Bill) but labels it a 'Select Committee.' The distinction — Select = one House, Joint = both Houses — is a high-frequency UPSC trap because both are Ad Hoc, both deal with Bills, and the names are superficially similar. A partially prepared student will focus on the correct function (examining a Bill) and miss the incorrect membership description.
solution.final_explanation:
The Select Committee and Joint Committee are the two Ad Hoc bill-scrutiny bodies, distinguished by their membership composition.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: A Select Committee consists of members from one House only. When members from both Houses jointly examine a Bill, it becomes a Joint Committee. The statement describes a Joint Committee but incorrectly names it a Select Committee.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Ad Hoc nature is the defining feature of both Select Committees and JPCs. Their existence concludes with the submission of their report.
• Statement 3 — Correct: JPCs have extensive powers — summoning witnesses (including Ministers and bureaucrats), calling for documents, recording evidence. Their findings are nonetheless recommendatory, not judicially enforceable.

Value Addition:
• Money Bills cannot be referred to either a Select Committee or a Joint Committee.
• The distinction between JPC (investigates specific matters) and Joint Committee on a Bill (examines specific legislation) is itself a frequent UPSC pairing question.
• JPCs are constituted by motion in one House, concurred by the other — a two-House consent mechanism.

solution.concept_anchor: BAC, Rules, Privileges, Ethics committee function mapping
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) swaps the functions of the BAC and Rules Committee (both are Speaker-chaired), which is the most common source of confusion for this topic.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Ethics vs Privileges distinction: Ethics deals with moral/professional conduct (D); Privileges deals with breach of legal rights and can recommend expulsion (C).
Distinguish BAC from Rules Committee: BAC allocates time for business (A); Rules Committee recommends amendments to procedural rules (B).
Confirm: A-2 (BAC → time allocation), B-1 (Rules → procedural amendments), C-4 (Privileges → breach and punishment), D-3 (Ethics → moral conduct).
This matches option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The BAC-Rules Committee conflation is the primary trap: both are chaired by the Speaker and deal with procedural aspects of parliamentary functioning. Students who vaguely remember 'Speaker-chaired procedural committee' cannot distinguish between the two without precise functional knowledge. The secondary trap is Ethics-Privileges confusion: both deal with member conduct, but privileges concern legal rights of the House, while ethics concerns moral/professional standards.
solution.final_explanation:
Four Speaker-proximate or conduct-related committees are frequently conflated in examination settings.

Correct pairings:
• A (BAC) — 2: Recommends allocation of time for government and other legislative business; scheduling, not rule-making.
• B (Rules Committee) — 1: Considers procedural matters and recommends amendments to the Rules of Procedure; approved by the full House.
• C (Privileges Committee) — 4: Investigates breach of privilege; can recommend reprimand, suspension, or expulsion; House passes the final order.
• D (Ethics Committee) — 3: Examines moral turpitude and professional misconduct; established in RS (1997) and LS (2000); not constitutionally mandated.

Trap pairings:
• BAC and Rules Committee: Both Speaker-chaired; distinguished by scheduling (BAC) vs rule-making (Rules Committee).
• Privileges and Ethics: Both deal with member conduct; distinguished by legal rights (Privileges) vs moral standards (Ethics).

Value Addition:
• BAC recommendations on scheduling are advisory — Speaker has final authority.
• Rules Committee amendments must receive full House approval.
• Ethics Committee is not constitutionally mandated; Privileges Committee draws from Articles 105/194.

solution.concept_anchor: Papers Laid on Table — procedural compliance only, not content
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both A and R are factually correct may select (a) without examining whether R actually explains why A is limited to procedural compliance.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Committee on Papers Laid on the Table scrutinises only the procedural compliance of tabling (timeliness, form, accompanying explanations) — not the substantive content of the papers.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Committee on Subordinate Legislation handles examination of rules and regulations framed under delegated authority. It is a separate committee with a distinct mandate.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — No. The existence of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation as a separate body does not explain why the Papers Laid on the Table committee is restricted to procedural compliance. A's limitation arises from its own defined mandate, not because another committee exists. R and A describe two separate institutional arrangements — they are not causally linked.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R are independently correct facts. The trap is in their causal relationship. R (existence of a separate Subordinate Legislation Committee) does not explain A (the Papers committee's procedural-only scope). A's limitation stems from its own mandate design — it was created to check tabling compliance, not to evaluate content. The existence of another committee is a parallel fact, not a cause. This is a classic 'both correct but causally unrelated' assertion-reason design.
solution.final_explanation:
Two scrutiny committees — Committee on Papers Laid on the Table and Committee on Subordinate Legislation — are often confused because both deal with executive-generated documents presented to Parliament.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The Committee on Papers Laid on the Table examines whether papers were tabled in time, in the correct format, and with required explanatory statements. It does not assess the merit, accuracy, or policy content of what is tabled. Its mandate is purely procedural compliance.

Reason (R) — Correct: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation is a distinct standing committee in each House that examines whether delegated legislation (rules, regulations, notifications) stays within the scope of the parent Act.

Causal link — Absent: R does not explain A. A's procedural-only scope is not caused by the existence of another committee — it reflects A's own definitional mandate. Both facts are true but independent.

Answer: Option (b) — Both A and R correct, but R does not explain A.

Value Addition:
• Both committees are standing committees existing separately in each House (not joint committees).
• Committee on Papers Laid on the Table checks: timeliness, form, and accompanying explanations — never substance.
• Committee on Subordinate Legislation checks: whether delegated rules exceed or contradict the parent Act.

solution.concept_anchor: CPU examines PSUs; DRSCs examine ministries — distinct jurisdictions
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know DRSCs examine ministry-related matters may assume the Ministry of Heavy Industries' DRSC covers PSUs under that ministry, conflating ministerial oversight with PSU-specific oversight.
elimination_logic: Identify the entity being examined: A Public Sector Undertaking (a government-owned enterprise) — not a ministry's policy or administration.
Eliminate option (a): DRSCs examine ministry Demands for Grants, Bills, and annual reports — not the internal operations of specific PSUs. PSU-specific examination is CPU's domain.
Eliminate option (c): The PAC examines government ministry accounts and CAG reports on ministries — not PSU operations directly. PSU audit reports go to CPU.
Eliminate option (d): A JPC is an Ad Hoc investigative body for specific matters of public importance — not for routine PSU operational examination.
Select option (b): CPU examines the working of Public Sector Undertakings and is the appropriate committee for PSU operational scrutiny.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The central confusion in this scenario is between the ministry that owns a PSU (Ministry of Heavy Industries) and the PSU itself. DRSCs examine ministries — the DRSC for Heavy Industries examines the ministry's Demands for Grants and annual reports. CPU examines the working of PSUs, including their CAG-audited accounts. Students who conflate 'ministry oversight' with 'PSU oversight' will incorrectly select option (a). The distinction is structural: DRSCs follow ministry lines; CPU follows ownership of PSUs.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between DRSC and CPU jurisdiction is a classic parallel oversight arrangement that generates examination confusion.

In this scenario, the relevant body is one that examines the working of a specific Public Sector Undertaking — its operations, efficiency, and CAG-audited accounts.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The DRSC for Heavy Industries examines the ministry's Demands for Grants and annual reports — not the internal workings of individual PSUs under it.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Committee on Public Undertakings (CPU) specifically examines the working of PSUs, including their CAG audit reports. This is precisely its mandate.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: PAC examines government ministry accounts — not PSU operations directly. PSU-related CAG reports are routed to CPU, not PAC.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: A JPC is an Ad Hoc investigative body for specific high-profile matters, not for routine PSU scrutiny.

Value Addition:
• CPU cannot examine PSUs in defence, atomic energy, or national security sectors.
• CPU also cannot review major government policy or day-to-day administration of PSUs.
• PAC examines ministries; CPU examines PSUs — both use CAG reports as their primary evidence base.

solution.concept_anchor: Committee proceedings secrecy and inter-session meetings

statement_analysis.statement: Parliamentary committee proceedings are secret, and members are prohibited from disclosing the evidence or deliberations of the committee before the report is presented to the House.
statement_analysis.reason: Secrecy of committee proceedings is a fundamental procedural rule. Members cannot publicly disclose evidence or deliberations until the report is formally presented to the House.

statement_analysis.statement: The quorum for parliamentary committees is the same as that for the full House — that is, one-half of total membership.
statement_analysis.reason: Committee quorum is one-third of total membership, which is distinctly lower than the one-half quorum required for the full House. This facilitates committee functioning with smaller attendance.

statement_analysis.statement: Departmentally Related Standing Committees can examine annual reports of constitutional bodies such as the Election Commission of India that fall under the relevant ministry cluster.
statement_analysis.reason: DRSCs cannot examine constitutional bodies' own legislation or administration. Constitutional and statutory bodies have a separate framework of accountability; DRSCs examine ministry-level reports and demands for grants, not the operations of autonomous constitutional bodies.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Selecting all three as correct is tempting because Statement 3 sounds procedurally correct — DRSCs do cover ministries, and constitutional bodies do 'fall under' administrative ministries.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Secrecy of committee proceedings is a standard procedural rule — disclosure before report presentation is prohibited. Statement 1 is Correct.
Verify Statement 2: Committee quorum is one-third, not one-half. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: DRSCs cannot examine constitutional bodies' own legislation or administration — their scope is ministry-level. Statement 3 is Incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the assumption that because an Election Commission falls under the administrative domain of the Law Ministry (for budget purposes), the DRSC for Law must be able to examine it. DRSCs explicitly cannot examine constitutional or statutory bodies' own functions and legislation. Statement 2 exploits the instinct to apply full House rules to committees — a persistent examination trap that appears in multiple question formats.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary committee procedures have several nuances that diverge from full House rules.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Secrecy is a fundamental protection for committee deliberations. Premature disclosure by a member constitutes a breach of privilege.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Committee quorum is one-third of membership. Full House quorum is one-half. The lower committee threshold facilitates continuous functioning even with limited attendance.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: DRSCs are explicitly barred from examining constitutional bodies' own legislation or administration. The Election Commission, CAG, UPSC, and similar bodies have separate accountability mechanisms outside the DRSC framework.

Value Addition:
• Witnesses before committees take an oath, and evidence is recorded — proceedings have a quasi-judicial character even though the committee itself is not a court.
• DRSCs examine ministry annual reports but not the annual reports or functioning of constitutional bodies under those ministries.
• Committee reports, once presented to the House, become public documents — secrecy ends at presentation.

solution.concept_anchor: BAC function — time allocation, not admissibility of questions
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) attributes the admissibility of questions function to the BAC, which sounds plausible because BAC deals with scheduling and questions are part of scheduled House business.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): BAC does not decide admissibility of questions — that is the Speaker's prerogative alone. Fabricated function.
Eliminate option (b): Committee on Government Assurances covers only floor assurances during debates and Question Hour — not Budget speech commitments. Incorrect pairing.
Eliminate option (d): Committee on Government Assurances does NOT have a joint committee structure across both Houses — separate committees exist in each House covering that House's proceedings only.
Select option (c): BAC is chaired by the Speaker and recommends allocation of time for government and other legislative business — correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the primary trap: it correctly identifies the BAC's chairperson (Speaker) and its general scheduling role but assigns it the function of admissibility of questions. Question admissibility is exclusively the Speaker's prerogative — not delegated to any committee. This plausible fabrication exploits the connection between the Speaker, the BAC, and parliamentary scheduling. Option (d) exploits the assumption that since Parliament has joint committees on many issues, Government Assurances might also be a joint committee — it is not.
solution.final_explanation:
The BAC and the Committee on Government Assurances each have precisely defined and limited functions.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: BAC allocates time for business; it does not decide admissibility of questions or notices. Admissibility is the Speaker's exclusive prerogative.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Committee on Government Assurances covers only oral and written assurances made during floor proceedings — not Budget speech commitments, which are policy documents.
• Option (c) — Correct: BAC is chaired by the Speaker (in LS) and recommends time allocation for government business and other legislative items. This is a correct and complete description.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Separate Committees on Government Assurances exist in each House — it is not a joint committee. Each covers only assurances given in its own House.

Value Addition:
• BAC recommendations are advisory — the Speaker has final authority on scheduling.
• BAC includes leaders of recognised parties and groups in the House.
• The Committee on Government Assurances tracks 'pending assurances' — those given but not yet implemented.

solution.concept_anchor: DRSC Bill referral discretionary; UK/US comparison

statement_analysis.statement: Reference of a Bill to a Departmentally Related Standing Committee is mandatory for all non-financial Bills under the Rules of Procedure of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: DRSC referral is discretionary — vested in the Speaker or Chairman, or by a House motion. It is not mandatory under any rule or constitutional provision. Major legislation has regularly bypassed DRSCs.

statement_analysis.statement: In the United Kingdom's parliamentary system, Select Committees have weaker formal powers than India's DRSCs, making the Indian committee system relatively stronger.
statement_analysis.reason: The comparative assessment is reversed: UK Select Committees are generally regarded as having greater influence and sharper oversight capacity than India's DRSCs. India's committee system is considered weaker by comparison, partly due to non-binding recommendations and declining Bill referrals.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Statement 1 is wrong but are uncertain about the UK comparison may assume Statement 2 reflects Indian pride in its committee system, selecting only Statement 1 as incorrect.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: DRSC referral is discretionary, not mandatory. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 2: UK Select Committees are stronger, not weaker, than Indian DRSCs. The statement reverses the correct comparative assessment. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Both statements are NOT correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits national pride and the surface plausibility of arguing India's committee system is stronger because DRSCs have quasi-judicial powers. The accurate comparative picture is that UK Select Committees are more influential, and US Congressional Committees are central to the legislative process in a way Indian DRSCs are not. The non-binding nature of recommendations and declining referral rates are key weaknesses. This reversed-comparison format is a recurring UPSC trick for international institution comparisons.
solution.final_explanation:
Both statements contain common misconceptions about the DRSC system that are reinforced by wishful thinking rather than empirical accuracy.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: DRSC referral is discretionary. The Speaker/Chairman decides, or the House passes a motion. Several landmark laws — including the CAA and Farm Laws — bypassed DRSC scrutiny entirely without any procedural violation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The comparison is inverted. UK Select Committees are widely regarded as having stronger oversight capacity than Indian DRSCs. US Congressional Committees are central to legislation in a way Indian committees are not. Indian DRSCs suffer from non-binding recommendations, low attendance, and declining Bill referrals.

Value Addition:
• PRS Legislative Research documented that between 2009 and 2014, about 71% of Bills were referred to DRSCs; this declined sharply in subsequent years.
• Second ARC recommended mandatory DRSC referral for all non-financial Bills as a reform measure.
• Strengthening committee systems — through mandatory referral, better staffing, and binding recommendations — is a key parliamentary reform demand.

solution.concept_anchor: Committee powers and recommendatory nature across specific committees

statement_analysis.statement: The Committee on Privileges can independently impose the punishment of expulsion on a member found guilty of breach of privilege, without requiring a House resolution.
statement_analysis.reason: The Committee on Privileges only investigates and recommends. The final order — including any punishment such as expulsion — must be passed by the full House through a resolution. The committee cannot act independently.

statement_analysis.statement: The Committee on Ethics was established in Rajya Sabha before it was established in Lok Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: Rajya Sabha established its Ethics Committee in 1997; Lok Sabha followed in 2000. Rajya Sabha was the pioneer in this institutional innovation.

statement_analysis.statement: The Joint Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes draws its members from both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a joint committee — it includes members from both Houses of Parliament, unlike the Estimates Committee which is exclusively a Lok Sabha body.

statement_analysis.statement: The Committee on Ethics in Lok Sabha is constituted under a specific provision of the Constitution of India.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ethics Committee is not constitutionally mandated. It was created through procedural rules and conventions — not by any article of the Constitution.

solution.strong_distractor: c — This IS the correct answer. The main distractor is option (b) — students who correctly identify Statements 2 and 3 but also incorrectly accept Statement 3 as the only correct one, or who doubt the RS-before-LS chronology for Ethics Committee, may waver.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Privileges Committee recommends; House passes the final order. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 2: RS Ethics Committee (1997) preceded LS Ethics Committee (2000). Statement 2 is Correct.
Verify Statement 3: Joint Committee on SC/ST Welfare draws from both Houses. Statement 3 is Correct.
Verify Statement 4: Ethics Committee is not constitutionally mandated — created through rules. Statement 4 is Incorrect.
Two statements (2 and 3) are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the assumption that a quasi-judicial committee with powers to recommend expulsion must itself be able to execute punishment. Statement 4 exploits the confusion between parliamentary privileges (which are constitutionally referenced under Articles 105/194) and the Ethics Committee (which is a rules-based creation). solution.final_explanation:

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Privileges Committee can only recommend — including expulsion. The House must pass a formal resolution. No committee can independently punish a member.

Value Addition:

• Both Ethics and Privileges committees have recommendatory authority only — the House retains final disciplinary power.
• Committee on Empowerment of Women is similarly structured to the SC/ST Welfare Committee — joint, recommendatory, no executive authority.

The trap places Estimates Committee before PAC in some options, exploiting the assumption that the Estimates Committee (which sounds more 'planning-era') came first.
